facts.title: Music for the Masses Tour Culmination (June 6, 1988)
facts.body: The tour promoting the "Music for the Masses" album concluded at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, where Depeche Mode demonstrated their breakthrough by filling the stadium with 60,000 people. This landmark performance was documented by both a live album and a concert film. "By the time the Music for the Mass is to erode into the Rose Bowl in Pasadena on June 6, 1988, the band was capable of filling a stadium with 60,000 people."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: California Raisins' Covers (1988)
facts.body: The California Raisins, characters who originated from popular animated advertisements, recorded a successful series of R&B cover albums. One of these albums achieved platinum status in 1988, demonstrating the commercial viability and widespread appeal of the R&B genre, even when performed by claymation figures. "the California raisins recorded a series of albums of R&B covers, went platinum in 1988."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Year-Long Sabbatical and Divorce (1988-1989)
facts.body: Madonna took 1988 off to address her "crumbling marriage" to Sean Penn, leading to their divorce by 1989, and to plan her next album. This period of inactivity, in hindsight, was not the end of her imperial phase but a strategic pause. "She took 1988 off to deal with her crumbling marriage to Sean Penn. They would divorce by 1989."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 2
facts.name: Madonna

facts.title: Official Naming (1988)

facts.title: Transition to Warner Brothers (April 8, 1988)
facts.body: By 1987, R.E.M. had outgrown IRS Records, which could no longer provide the necessary distribution and support for their expanding fanbase. Warner Brothers, a major label, offered a $6 million check and promises of complete creative control, leading R.E.M. to sign on April 8, 1988. This move was considered risky for their image with their fanbase, but was deemed necessary for worldwide record distribution and to get off the constant recording and touring treadmill. "R.E.M. became the biggest of the so-called college rock indie bands to make the jump to a multi-million dollar major record label."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Major Label Deal with Warner Bros. (1988)
facts.body: R.E.M. made the strategic decision to transition from an indie alternative/college rock band to a major label, feeling exhausted by the constant recording and touring demands. Following a bidding war, Warner Brothers signed them in 1988 for an unprecedented $6 million, an exceptionally large sum for an indie band at that time. Eight years later, they secured another deal worth $80 million, demonstrating their significant market value and influence. "Warner signed them in 1988 for $6 million, an insanely huge number for an indie band at that time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Major Label Signing (1988)
facts.body: By 1987, R.E.M. felt they had exhausted their potential as an indie band and faced a choice between a career stall or signing with a major label. They signed with Warner Brothers on April 8, 1988, receiving a $6 million check. Michael Stipe stated the move was necessary for "worldwide" distribution, as IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit. Peter Buck reflected on the band's ongoing struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial moves, acknowledging they were "part of the machine." "So it came to pass on April 8, 1988, R.E.M. signed with Warner Brothers and took home a $6 million check."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Evolution from 1988 to Present
facts.body: The period from 1988 onwards has been a significant time for industrial music fans, with the genre evolving from its primitive clanging and banging into a sophisticated amalgam of metal, distortion, percussion, samplers, and synthesizers. While its widespread popularity from the 1990s has diminished, it remains a distinct and hard-edged musical form. "It's evolved from the primitive clang and banging into something very sophisticated. It's an amalgam of metal, distortion, percussion, samplers, and synthesizers."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: "Second Act" Breakthrough (Age 54, 1988)
facts.body: Leonard Cohen experienced a major career resurgence, or "second act," in 1988 at age 54 with the album *I'm Your Man*. Columbia Records successfully marketed him to the alternative rock crowd, leading to global stardom that far surpassed his initial career fame. "And it all began, or began again, if you want, with a record by a 54-year-old that was marketed to 20-somethings in 1988."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Late Bloomers
facts.name: Leonard Cohen

facts.title: Disastrous Live Interview (1988)
facts.body: In 1988, while on air, the speaker interviewed Leonard Cohen, who was 55 years old and being relaunched by IRS Records as an alternative artist. The speaker, unaware of Cohen's stature as a respected writer, poet, and songwriter whose work was studied at PhD level, was unprepared. Cohen, dressed in all black and smoking "terrible, detained cigarettes," responded poorly when the speaker tried to call him "Lenny," blowing smoke in his face and sternly replying "Don't." The interview was short and unsuccessful, attributed by the speaker to his own lack of knowledge and propriety. "So he comes in and he's all dressed in black hair, black sunglasses, black clothes, black shoes. And he's smoking these terrible, detained cigarettes, these French cigarettes that's stunk."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording
facts.name: Leonard Cohen

facts.title: Donington Park Crowd Collapse (1988)
facts.body: During Guns N' Roses' set at a large outdoor show at Donington Park racetrack in England on August 28, 1988, a crowd collapse occurred. facts.body: In 1988, Frank Zappa called the then 17-year-old John Frusciante to offer him a gig in his band. However, Frusciante decided against joining because Zappa "wouldn't condone anyone who used illegal drugs in his band," a condition Frusciante was unwilling to meet at the time. "Frank Zappa called, but since Zappa wouldn't condone anyone who used illegal drugs in his band, John decided that he'd better not go."

facts.title: Sublime (Long Beach, 1988) – Co-Headlined First Vans Warped Tour 1995; Singer Brad Nowell Died of Heroin Overdose Two Months Before Major Label Album Came Out
facts.body: Sublime came together in 1988 and had their own label (Skunk Records) by 1992. They became wildly popular by playing anywhere and everywhere, co-headlining the first Vans Warped Tour in 1995 and the first Sno-Core tour. facts.title: R.E.M. Signing (April 8, 1988)
facts.body: Warner Brothers, a major record label, successfully signed R.E.M. on April 8, 1988, offering a significant $6 million check and a promise of complete creative control. This move was pivotal as R.E.M. became the largest college rock indie band to transition to a multi-million dollar major label, seeking expanded distribution and an end to their constant touring cycle. "So when Warner's came with that $6 million check on April the 8th, 1988, they signed."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8
facts.name: Warner Brothers (distributed Rancid, who were influenced by Operation Ivy and labelmates with Bad Religion on Epitaph, demonstrating industry connections)

facts.title: Major Label Signing of R.E.M. (1988)
facts.body: Warner Brothers signed R.E.M. in 1988 for an initial sum of $6 million after a bidding war, which was an exceptionally large amount for an indie band at that time. Eight years later, they renewed the deal for $80 million, signifying R.E.M.'s commercial success and influence in the music industry. "Warner signed them in 1988 for $6 million, an insanely huge number for an indie band at that time."

facts.title: Near-Miss Lockerbie Bombing (1988)
facts.body: John Lydon, of the Sex Pistols and Public Image Limited, came very close to dying in the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988. He and his wife, Nora, had seats on the flight but missed it by minutes due to his wife taking too long to pack, which caused a big fight, and then getting stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow Airport. "Johnny Leiden with public image limited and death disco. He came very, very close to dying in the Lockerbie bombing in December of 1988."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Missed Pan Am Flight 103 (1988)
facts.body: Johnny Lydon and his wife, Nora, narrowly missed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, which was later bombed over Lockerbie, Scotland. Delays caused by Nora taking too long to pack, a subsequent argument, and getting stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow Airport meant they missed the flight by minutes, thus saving their lives. "Nora, his wife, took too long to pack. They had a big fight, which delayed them even more, and then they got stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow. They missed their flight by minutes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Airplanes!
facts.name: John Lydon

facts.title: Missed Pan Am Flight 103 (1988)
facts.body: The R&B group The Four Tops had seats booked on Pan Am Flight 103 for December 21, 1988. "The four tops, the R&B group, had seats but they overslept after performing on BBC's top of the pops the night before."

facts.title: Pivotal Role in Frusciante Joining RHCP (1988)
facts.body: Flea played a key role in John Frusciante joining the Red Hot Chili Peppers. After a jam session with Frusciante at Flea's apartment, Flea was so impressed that he immediately called Anthony Kiedis, stating, "this kid has got to be in our band." "But the chemistry with Flea was good. They held a jam session just the two of them at Flea's apartment, and once that was over, Flea called Anthony and said, this kid has got to be in our band."

facts.title: Struggles with Sobriety (1988-1992)
facts.body: Following Hillel Slovak's death in 1988, Anthony Kiedis was working hard to maintain his sobriety after a "drugs and alcohol bender." His efforts to stay away from heroin, coke, and alcohol led him to distance himself from John Frusciante, whose teenage partying lifestyle was at odds with Kiedis's recovery. He continued to face "continuing sobriety struggles" during the band's turmoil in 1992. "Anthony was working hard to be sober after going on a drugs and alcohol bender after Hillel died."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1

While the speaker notes it's a "master album" with "epic moments," they also express that it might not be substantially better than earlier works like *Confusion Is Sex* or *Sister*. Its success led to two major changes: the band gained greater cachet, allowing them to live comfortably from their music, and they signed with Geffen Records. "Redding Nation es el éxito que los catapulta y los saca un poco de esos círculos underground."

facts.title: Ahead of Their Time in 1988
facts.body: In 1988, the broader music world was not yet ready for Mudhoney's sound and attitude, as rock music was still dominated by hair metal and alternative rock remained largely marginalized. Additionally, Seattle was considered off the beaten track, hindering recognition. "More importantly, music at large wasn't really ready for this sound and attitude. Things were still all about hair metal in 1988. Rock music was still dominant, and any kind of alt rock was still very much in the margins. Besides, Seattle was way off the beaten track in those days, and no one paid attention to what was happening there."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Debut Album
facts.body: The debut album by The Pixies is titled *Surfer Rosa*, which directly references surf culture and the band's subtle surf influences. "The name of the Pixies debut album is Surfer Rosa."

facts.name: Surfer Rosa

facts.title: Debut Studio Album
facts.body: Steve Albini produced *Surfer Rosa*, the first full-length studio album for the then-unknown Pixies in 1988. The album instantly established the band as pioneers of American indie music and was widely regarded as Album of the Year by many media outlets. Its sound was remarkably distinctive, being innovative, experimental, contagious, luminous, and raw in equal measure, and the band never achieved such a strong and thrilling sound again. "En 1988, Steve Albindli producería unos entonces desconocidos Pixies en el que sería su primilalbum largo de estudio, surferrosa."
facts.source: Central Sonora

facts.title: Shoegaze Precursor
facts.body: Released in 1988, this record is considered to have arrived "at the very beginning of the whole shoegaze thing." It was characterized by "guitar drones and layers and layers of feedback" that generated a "near-trance-like soundscape," an "impenetrable atmosphere of sound," and made extensive use of effects pedals. "In 1988, they released a record called, Isn't Anything, which was filled with guitar drones and layers and layers of feedback that created near-translikes soundscape."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: History of Shoegaze
facts.name: Isn’t Anything

facts.title: Debut Album
facts.body: Released in 1988, this album, along with the "You Made Me Realise" EP, marked a significant period for the band. Released only four months apart, these two works showcased My Bloody Valentine beginning to find their distinctive sound, characterized by extreme experimentation with guitars, extensive use of effects pedals, and the integration of noise as a natural component of their music. These works were very well received within the community and were considered the almost official starting point for the emerging sound of Shoegaze. "Estos trabajos fueron muy bien acogidos dentro de la comunidad y serían considerados como el punto de partida casi oficial de este sonido que estaba emergiendo. El Show Guys."
facts.source: Central Sonora

facts.body: This album, released in 1988, marked a pivotal moment in the timeline of rap, leaving American society quite disoriented. Formed out of necessity in the mid-80s due to the extensive Afro-American hip hop scene, the band broke a generational gap and established themselves as absolute leaders of the "gangsta movement." The album is characterized by its rage, aggression, and violence, serving as a therapeutic reflection of the harsh realities lived in Afro-American suburbs. It explicitly discusses racist police behavior, indiscriminate arrests, and police violence, with some band members having personally suffered arbitrary detentions. It also explores the crude and direct relationship of Afro-American suburbs with drugs, detailing both those who profited and those who were devastated and victimized. The album created a "convulsion" in the United States, resonating deeply with many Afro-American youths who identified more with its discourse than with the more restrained messages of older generations. Its release caused significant discomfort, even for the police, due to its direct attacks on law enforcement and calls for popular uprising. It is considered an important, politically complex album and a faithful representation of Afro-American society in the late 80s. "Y aparecieron en 1988 con el grandísimo album Straight, Abra Kampton, que marcaba un antes y un después en la línea temporal del rap y que dejaba la sociedad a América nabastante descolocada."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: NWA y el inicio del Gangsta Rap. Las letras polémicas no son nuevas.
facts.name: Straight Outta Compton

facts.title: "Needle Time" Restriction (Introduced Year not specified, removed 1988)
facts.body: The BBC implemented "Needle Time," a deal with the musician's union that restricted the amount of commercially recorded music it could play during any 24-hour period. This policy, which ensured the BBC would play either live music or recordings made in its own studios, was in effect until 1988, and as recently as 1967, only allowed five hours a day of commercial records. "For example, this marked the beginning of something called Needle Time with the BBC, which was a deal with the musician's union. It restricted the BBC to playing only a certain amount of recorded music during any 24-hour period, thereby ensuring that the BBC would play either live music or recordings the BBC made themselves in their studios or elsewhere."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years
facts.name: BBC

facts.title: Death from Heroin Overdose (June 25, 1988)
facts.body: Hillel Slovak, the guitarist for the Red Hot Chili Peppers, died of a heroin overdose on June 25, 1988, while the band was working on a new album. His death led to drummer Jack Irons quitting the band due to his inability to cope. "But then Hilarl died of a heroin overdose on June 25, 1988, as the band was working on a new album."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1

facts.title: Major Label Debut
facts.body: "Green" was R.E.M.'s first album released on Warner Brothers, a major record label, after their significant move from indie label IRS Records. The album was symbolically important because it demonstrated that a college rock indie band could transition to a major label without compromising their music, art, or integrity. Its title was theorized to be a humorous nod to their major label signing. "The Green album was hugely important in a symbolic sense. It showed that it was possible for a college rock indie band to work for a major without selling their music, their art, and their integrity."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8
facts.name: Green

facts.title: First Major Label Album
facts.body: Released in 1988, this was R.E.M.'s sixth album and their first as a major label band after five independent releases. It performed well, reaching the top 20 in Canada, the US, and Australia, and the top 30 in the UK, setting high expectations for its follow-up. "This was the follow-up to 1998's Green album, which was their first record as a major label band."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Amazing Year That Was 1991
facts.name: Green

facts.title: First Warner Brothers Album
facts.body: This album was R.E.M.'s first release after signing with Warner Brothers. The band named the album "Green" as a subtle, humorous nod to their perceived "selling out" by moving to a major label, while still maintaining creative control. "Why do you think that first record for Warner Brothers is called Green?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1
facts.name: Green

facts.title: "Great Trilogy" Album
facts.body: This album is widely regarded as the first installment in R.E.M.'s "great trilogy" of albums released with Warner Music. This collection of works is considered one of the best trilogies in the history of US music, signifying a new era for the band after their departure from IRS Records. "sería el green, el out of time y el automátil, for the people."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El papel de REM en los '80

facts.body: This album was being promoted in 1988 when IRS Records decided to relaunch Leonard Cohen's career as an alternative artist, leading to an ill-fated live radio interview. "And he had this album called I'm Your Man."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording
facts.name: I’m Your Man

facts.body: This album, released in 1988 when Cohen was 54, was strategically marketed by Columbia Records to an open-minded alternative rock audience, leading to tremendous critical and commercial success through airplay on alternative radio and producing three singles. "The album was called I'm Your Man, and it was a tremendous critical and commercial success, something that was built through airplay on alternative radio."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Late Bloomers
facts.name: I’m Your Man

facts.body: This album, released in 1988, marked a significant breakthrough for Leonard Cohen into the alternative music world, becoming a hit. It features the song "First We Take Manhattan," which showcases his characteristically low baritone voice. "Leonard made a strange breakthrough into the alternative world in 1988 when his album, I'm Your Man, became a hit."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: I’m Your Man

facts.body: This album, released in 1988, represented an unexpected breakthrough for Leonard Cohen into the alternative music world, achieving significant success. "Leonard made a strange breakthrough into the alternative world in 1988 when his album I'm Your Man became a hit."

facts.body: Released in 1988, Living Colour's debut album was a groundbreaking "eye opening, ear opening, mind expanding experience" for many listeners. It masterfully blended diverse genres including metal, punk, soul, jazz, and rap, earning them recognition as MTV heroes and multiple Grammy Awards. "In 1988, they released a debut album entitled Vivid, and for many, this was an eye opening, ear opening, mind expanding experience."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 90s Part 5a: Hip-Hop's Effects Part 1
facts.name: Vivid

facts.body: This debut album, released in 1988, launched Living Color into prominence, leading to significant touring and accolades. "Their debut album was called Vivid, and after it came out in 1988, Living Color took off."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Vivid

facts.title: Acting Role in "Igla" (1988)
facts.body: In 1988, Victor Tsoy demonstrated his martial arts abilities in the cult film "Igla" (The Needle). In this movie, Tsoy's character confronts a corrupt world, fighting against drug dealers, drug addiction, and the challenging times they lived in. By this point, he was already a star. "Años más tarde, en 1968, puedo demostrar sus habilidades en la película de Culto Igla. En esta película, Victor Tsoy se enfrenta un mundo corrupto, luchando contra los escapos de la droga, la misma droga adicción y los tiempos que han tocado vivir."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Viktor Tsoi. El padre del Postpunk Ruso
facts.name: Viktor Tsoi

facts.title: Stardom Cemented by "Igla" (1988)
facts.body: The premiere of the film "Igla" in 1988 definitively cemented Victor Tsoy's status as a star, solidifying his reputation as the greatest rock star Russia has ever had. "El otroito de ese año fue el estreno de la mencionada película Iglá, que le acabó convertiendo definitivamente en una estrella."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Viktor Tsoi. El padre del Postpunk Ruso
facts.name: Viktor Tsoi

facts.body: The sessions for this album, produced by Steve Lillywhite, included early attempts to record "Fairy Tale of New York" with Shane McGowan singing both male and female parts. Lillywhite later brought the rough cut to his wife, Kirsty MacColl, for her to record the female vocals. "Those sessions were part of what became the Pogs' third album, which was called If I Should Fall From Grace With God."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This second album by Fishbone is recommended for listeners unfamiliar with the band, featuring songs like "Ma and Pa." The band became a significant part of the West Coast alternative scene by 1988, bridging the second wave of Ska with the upcoming third wave. "If you're unfamiliar with Fishbone, dig into their second album Truth and Soul, which featured songs like this. It's Ma and Pa."

facts.title: Missed Pan Am Flight 103 (1988)
facts.body: Johnny Lydon and his wife, Nora, narrowly missed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, which was later bombed over Lockerbie, Scotland. Delays caused by Nora taking too long to pack, a subsequent argument, and getting stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow Airport meant they missed the flight by minutes, thus saving their lives. "Nora, his wife, took too long to pack. They had a big fight, which delayed them even more, and then they got stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow. They missed their flight by minutes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Airplanes!
facts.name: Johnny Lydon

facts.body: Released in 1988, this album is identified as a potential "inflection point" for skate punk, marking a shift towards more melodic music with actual singable melodies, while retaining speed and intensity. Following this record, most bands in the genre adopted a direction with more "pop sensibilities." "The inflection point might have been Bad Religions 1988 album Suffer."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
